distractors_rationale: This is a common misinterpretation. The p-value is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true — it is P(data | H₀), not P(H₀ | data). The probability of H₀ given the data depends on the Bayesian prior.

Correct. The p-value is defined as: the probability of obtaining a result as extreme as or more extreme than the observed result, ASSUMING the null hypothesis is true. It is P(observed or more extreme data | H₀ is true). This is a frequentist probability about the DATA under a hypothetical null distribution, not a probability about the hypothesis.
This is another common misinterpretation. P(alternative | data) = 1 - P(null | data), and since we cannot directly derive P(null | data) from a p-value, this statement is incorrect.

The false positive rate (Type I error rate) for a study design is the long-run frequency α (here, implied as 0.05). The p-value for an individual study is NOT the false positive rate for that specific finding. In fact, the false positive rate for a 'significant' finding depends on the prior probability of the hypothesis (see Ioannidis 2005).
The p-value is about data extremeness under the null, not about the proportion of patients affected.
teaching_point: Common p-value misinterpretations (Goodman 2008, Wasserstein & Lazar 2016): (1) P-value is NOT the probability that H₀ is true — it assumes H₀ is true. (2) P-value is NOT the false positive rate — the false positive rate depends on prior probability and is typically much higher than 0.05 (Ioannidis' 'most published research findings are false' argument: PPV = (1 − β) × R / (1 − β × R + α), where R = ratio of true to false hypotheses). (3) 1 − p is NOT the probability that H₁ is true. (4) p = 0.04 does not mean there is only a 4% chance the result is a false positive. ASA statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016): p-values do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true, nor the size of an effect. MRCPsych: be prepared to identify the correct definition of a p-value.
source: Wasserstein & Lazar 2016 (Am Stat); Goodman 2008 (Am J Med)

stem: A survey study reports that 40% of psychiatrists experience burnout using a validated questionnaire scoring scale. The margin of error is reported as ±3% at 95% confidence. The sample size was approximately 1,067. If the researchers wanted to reduce the margin of error to ±2% at the same confidence level, approximately how many participants would be needed?
options: 1,067 (the same — margin of error cannot be reduced)
distractors_rationale: This is approximately n for ±2.5% margin — not quite ±2%.

Correct. For a proportion p = 0.40, the margin of error (95% CI) ≈ 1.96 × √(p(1-p)/n). To reduce the margin from 3% to 2% (a 1.5× reduction), the sample size must increase by (1.5)² = 2.25×. 1,067 × 2.25 = 2,401 ≈ 2,400. More precisely: n = (1.96² × p(1-p)) / d² = (3.84 × 0.24) / 0.02² = 0.9216 / 0.0004 = 2,304. The general rule: to halve the margin of error, you need 4× the sample size. For a reduction from 3% to 2%, the factor is (3/2)² = 2.25.
This would be 4× for halving the margin (from 3% to 1.5%), not from 3% to 2%.
Sample size directly affects the margin of error — increasing n reduces the margin of error in proportion to √n.
Reducing n would increase the margin of error, not decrease it.
teaching_point: Sample size for survey precision: margin of error (MOE) = z_α/₂ × √(p(1-p)/n). The MOE is proportional to 1/√n — to halve the MOE, quadruple n. For a proportion near 0.5, p(1-p) is maximised (0.25) → most conservative sample size estimate. MRCPsych: survey methodology questions often test the relationship between sample size and precision. The rule: n ∝ 1/MOE². Common in epidemiological and cross-sectional study questions.
subdomain: Statistics — Sample Size & Margin of Error
source: Kirkwood & Sterne 2003

stem: A Bayesian analysis of an antidepressant trial reports a Bayes Factor (BF₁₀) of 8.5. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The data are 8.5 times more likely under H₁ (effect exists) than under H₀ (no effect)
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true is 8.5 times the probability that the null is true
There is an 85% probability that the antidepressant is effective
The p-value is approximately 0.12
The effect is clinically significant
distractors_rationale: Correct. BF₁₀ = p(data | H₁) / p(data | H₀). BF₁₀ = 8.5 means the observed data are 8.5 times more likely under the alternative hypothesis (that a true effect exists) than under the null hypothesis (no effect). This represents 'moderate' to 'strong' evidence by Jeffreys' criteria: BF 3-10 = moderate evidence, BF 10-30 = strong evidence, BF 30-100 = very strong. A Bayes Factor is a likelihood ratio comparing the predictive adequacy of two hypotheses — it does NOT directly give the posterior probability of H₁ (which requires specifying the prior probability of H₁).

The posterior odds = BF₁₀ × prior odds. If the prior odds were 1:1 (prior probability of H₁ = 50%), then posterior odds = 8.5:1, meaning posterior probability of H₁ = 8.5/(1+8.5) = 89.5%. But the BF itself is not the posterior odds — it multiplies the prior odds. Many MRCPsych candidates confuse BF with posterior odds.
Without specifying the prior probability of H₁, we cannot derive this probability. The BF is a likelihood ratio, not a probability.

BF and p-value cannot be directly converted. p-values depend on sample size and stopping rules; BF depends on the prior distribution. A BF of 8.5 might correspond to p ≈ 0.02-0.03 for a typical sample, but the exact relationship is not fixed.
The BF provides evidence FOR an effect but does not quantify the magnitude or clinical significance of the effect.
teaching_point: Bayes Factor (BF): likelihood ratio for H₁ vs H₀. BF₁₀ = p(data | H₁) / p(data | H₀). BF > 3 indicates moderate evidence for H₁; BF > 10 strong; BF > 30 very strong. Advantages over p-values: (1) Can quantify evidence FOR the null (BF < 1/3 provides evidence for H₀ — p-values cannot do this); (2) Not distorted by early stopping; (3) Scale is continuous (3-10 is moderate, not a binary 'significant/not significant'). Jeffreys' (1939/1961) criteria: BF > 100 = decisive, 30-100 = very strong, 10-30 = strong, 3-10 = moderate, 1-3 = anecdotal, < 1/3 = moderate evidence for H₀. MRCPsych: know the BF interpretation and its advantages over p-values.
source: Jeffreys 1961; Kass & Raftery 1995 (JASA); Rouder et al 2009
